texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crz9:
Stretching across the Kerch Strait in the Black Sea, the Crimean Bridge was always a symbol: for Russia, a prestige project cementing its claim to sovereign Ukrainian territory, and for Ukraine, a hated piece of infrastructure emblematic of Moscow's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula.
A key section of the double-arched, 12-mile-long bridge now lies on the seabed, brought down by an arsenal of Ukrainian long-range weaponry in a seven-stage operation culminating in a dramatic collapse.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said that the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But eight years after its unveiling, the bridge has now become material proof of Kyiv's ability to pierce through Moscow's military defences to hit even its most treasured and protected structures.
The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.
For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November , when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.
One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.
The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.
The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.
Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.
Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.
This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.
The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.
But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.
Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.
The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".
Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".
Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.
There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.
In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.
Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq78:
Masha was in her kitchen when she heard the explosions blast through the city
The alarms warning of a ballistic missile threat went off just before 23:30 on Monday in Kyiv. Moments later came the boom of explosions.
Once again, the main bridges over the broad River Dnipro that cuts through the city were the target and this time the Russian missiles hit what they wanted.
Close to one end of the Pivnichnyi (Northern) bridge there is a large crater and in the pouring rain, water now rushes through it to the river below. Chunks of tarmac and metal are scattered around.
At its broadest point, the jagged hole is about eight metres wide.
The crossing is closed to all traffic apart from the occasional fire engine or police car passing at high speed. By contrast, nearby roads are jammed with cars and trucks, forced to take long detours.
Anyone in a hurry to move around this city has to walk, or cycle, across the bridge, picking their way through the wreckage. In the miserable weather, that also means getting very wet.
Masha and her family moved to a flat next to the bridge because they had been living by a power plant that kept getting hit by Russian missiles.
Last night, she was in the kitchen of their new place when the Russians struck the bridge. She thought her windows would be blown out of their frames by the explosions.
"It was really scary. We had no idea they'd hit here so much. It's like we're cursed," Masha told me, describing grabbing her child and running into the corridor for protection.
"It's difficult, but we're used to it. And we try to take the positive from everything. Like: we survived today! So we can be happy about that."
The Northern Bridge crossing is closed to traffic while emergency response teams work to clear the debris
From the damage, it looks like Russia targeted the same spot on the bridge with a volley of three missiles, aiming to keep the road closed for as long as possible.
A major recovery operation is under way, with firefighters and engineers in fluorescent overalls working to evaluate the extent of the damage. But it looks like the disruption will continue for some time.
Further along the Dnipro River, the Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was also hit on Monday night, with four missiles.
The metro line across it was suspended for a while, although by mid-afternoon it had been restored. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said road transport in one direction was also being partially restored.
On the Pivnichnyi bridge, a man with a bag of tennis rackets on his back was gazing at the crater in front of him. He was heading home from the courts after he had travelled on foot to the left bank.
"It is upsetting," Anatolii told us. "Then when you read the news of what our side did to the Crimea bridge, you do feel a bit better."
The main bridges over the River Dnipro - that cuts through Kyiv - were the target of Russian strikes
That is because there was a battle of the bridges overnight.
Ukrainian missiles hit the one Russia had built to occupied Crimea, and caused serious damage. That bridge is prized by Russian President Vladimir Putin personally, a symbol of his illegal 2014 takeover.
Ukrainians loathe it for the same reason and now a section has collapsed into the sea, along with its towering arch.
To many here, the timing feels significant: a blow to Putin's image, just as he wants to seem most powerful at this week's summit with the US and China.
But for Kyiv resident Antonina, today is just another challenge to overcome.
The 67-year-old, who we met pulling a shopping trolley through the debris on a bridge in the Ukrainian capital, was heading to see her son on the right bank, but taxi drivers were charging a fortune to go round, so she decided to walk.
"It was a very scary night. It felt like something exploded right over my head. We will get through this, but I just wish the war would end."

Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump
Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.
The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing , one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe .
The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.
Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.
That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.
Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.
It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.
Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.
Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.
Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.
If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.
A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.
The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.
Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

US officials ‘debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute’ plot to detonate a ‘dirty bomb’, report says
Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there were “no credible threats” at this time.
Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”
After a CNN report , citing seven unnamed US officials, that new US intelligence suggested Iran was working on plans that would use a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, or a chemical weapon against senior Trump administration officials.
The report noted, however, that US officials “continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot”.
The US president’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular among Americans. His Republican party was widely rejected by voters in the midterm elections, in which the GOP lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Asked in the Philippines on Tuesday if there was reason to believe that such an Iranian attack was imminent, Trump said: “If there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to ​be crazy.”
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement: “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
CNN cited the unnamed officials as saying that Tehran’s planning was an effort by Iran to “give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack”, but the plans include specific locations and targets.
While the plans would signify that Iran is willing to escalate its tactics against the US, there is no evidence to suggest they will go ahead with them.
The US and Israel went to war with Iran starting in February, with early airstrikes killing Iranian officials, including the supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war will be over soon, but it has continued.
The US president has argued that US involvement in the war is necessary so that the country does not build nuclear weapons. Iran has blocked trade through the strait of Hormuz, creating rising fuel costs – and rattling the global economy.

A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign beneath a billboard depicting a launched missile, a man with a rifle, people and current and the late Revolutionary Guard missile force commanders with clenched fists, with a sign which reads in Farsi: "The sky is a place for our pride and loyalty," in downtown Tehran, Iran, Monday. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption
CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.
Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.
The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
This is a locator map for the Gulf Cooperation Council member states: Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and United Arab Emirates. AP hide caption
Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.
Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.
"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."
With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.
The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.
Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.
"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."
Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
Israeli lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana as the new parliament speaker , marking a step towards reversing domestic policies from the outgoing government led by Benjamin Netanyahu.
Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot – the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu – was voted in on Tuesday, receiving 66 votes in the 120-member chamber.
Netanyahu’s Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate. He received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
The Israel parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
“I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender,” said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of Netanyahu’s domestic agenda, especially regarding contentious reforms to the judiciary.
Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, having been in and out of office for three decades.
The vote took place weeks after October 27 parliamentary elections in which neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the Knesset, with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu’s hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot’s candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s parties met on Sunday to discuss the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume the war on Iran, has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu’s legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel’s security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services, during which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.
Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot’s efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.
As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.

A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean.
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

The E1 area east of Jerusalem is a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in “illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians” in the West Bank .
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers .
Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

Matan Kahana, a former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu.
The Israeli parliament, or Knesset , elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.
The parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
Read more Eisenkot pushes October 7 inquiry as Netanyahu targets Arab parties in tense new parliament
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu, Israel 's longest serving prime minister who has been in and out of office for three decades.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the 120-member Knesset in October 27 elections , with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
The vote for parliament speaker crystallised their standoff, with a heated debate before the vote.
In October, Eisenkot's wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu's finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot's candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
"I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender," said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Netanyahu's and Eisenkot's parties met Sunday on the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume war on Iran , has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
Eisenkot said afterwards that Netanyahu was unfit to "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute" after an explosive media report that his allies tried to make up allegations of fraud to frame lawmakers from the Arab minority.
On Tuesday, Israel's central elections committee released a statement regarding the ongoing investigation into the fraud accusations led by the Shin Bet intelligence agency.
"At this stage, there is no evidence that bribes were paid to voters on a scale that could have affected the election results," it said.
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu's legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
The judicial reforms initiated shortly after Netanyahu began his latest term in December 2022 triggered some of Israel's largest ever protests, bringing tens of thousands to the streets, with liberals fearing an erosion of the country's democracy.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas 's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services in which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.
Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot's efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.
As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.
The parliament speaker serves as acting head of state when the president is unable to perform his duties.

Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu .
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot , the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu .
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.
They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death
A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
Suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.
Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.
He said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.
But the United States attorney general, Todd Blanche, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Donald Trump.
“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” said Blanche after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.
“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”
US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.
Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.

CCTV footage posted on social media, verified by Reuters and in part by the BBC, appears to shows the plane crash
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

Daithi O’Corrain charged with destruction of US government property, after allegedly smashing gauges and cutting hydraulic lines
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks.
O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland , according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan.
He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.
The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules, which had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said.
O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged with causing criminal damage and trespassing.
Manhattan US attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets – and thus our national security – will not be tolerated.”
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends said he disarmed the C-130 in protest against the US’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza.
O’Corrain plotted the attack on 11 April for months, US prosecutors said.
He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking on to the airport’s grounds, prosecutors allege.
O’Corrain subscribed to a phone app that provided live flight tracking and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors added.
He is also accused of trying to contact someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon airport, prosecutors said.
O’Corrain breached the airport’s perimeter at about 4.40 am and broke into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
The document added he used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed.
He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and put ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said: “This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism.”

The US has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus has spread at the fastest rate in more than 30 years, while Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles-elimination status. Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases, in the US and globally, and measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024.
The US has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread – largely among the unvaccinated – at the highest rate in more than 30 years.
Mexico also lost its measles-elimination status, following a resurgence of the virus there that included a massive outbreak in Chihuahua state. Bolivia , too, lost its status.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) declaration has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but it marks a sharp turnabout in a disease largely controlled through decades of scientific advances. It also may be seen as the beginning of an era in which diseases of the past become deadly problems for the modern world.
“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director, said at a news conference. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.”
PAHO expects the US, Bolivia and Mexico to submit plans "in the coming weeks” for how each country will go about trying to stop transmission for at least a year and regain measles elimination status, Dr. Daniel Salas, the organization's executive manager for immunisations, told reporters.
Measles has been spreading throughout the Americas since 2024. The outbreaks in North America started in close-knit Mennonite communities and have since spread to areas with low vaccination rates. Last year, Canada lost its measles-free designation for the first time since 1998 .
International health officials consider measles eliminated when the virus is not locally spreading among residents. The designation hinges on whether a single measles chain has spread uninterrupted for at least 12 months.
Tuesday's announcement signals an erosion of public health preparedness.
Vaccination rates have been falling against a number of diseases , in the US and globally. And as one of the most infectious diseases known to medicine, measles was seen as likely to be one of the first vaccine-preventable diseases to reemerge when vaccinations falter.
“It can be the canary in the coal mine to other things,” said Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials.
Measles vaccine have safely stopped the virus’ spread in the US for 30 years.
It takes a community vaccination rate of 95% to prevent outbreaks, experts say. But as fewer parents vaccinate their children and federal leaders sow doubt and confusion about the importance of getting vaccinated, the virus has found footholds in communities across the US. All but three states have reported a confirmed case of measles this year.

The last two years have been the worst in a generation in the US, with more than 7,000 cases and 13 reported deaths. Nearly all of those people were either unvaccinated or didn’t report whether they were vaccinated. More than 10% of those infected had to be hospitalized.
The illness typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults over age 30.
Ten measles-associated deaths have been reported in the US this year, making it the deadliest in more than three decades. Health officials haven't released detailed information on each death, but at least five of the dead were children.
Since the US eliminated measles in 2000, public health officials usually logged fewer than 200 cases a year, most of them tied to international travel.
But since 2025, measles has sickened thousands. It started with a major outbreak in the Southwest.
In Texas, more than 760 people got sick and two children died . In New Mexico, about 100 people got sick and one adult died. Then measles exploded in rural border towns in Arizona and Utah, followed by a major outbreak in South Carolina in the winter and spring that sickened nearly 1,000 people.
This year has been much worse – the worst for measles cases since 1991. The more than 5,400 confirmed cases so far this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that dwarfed the earlier ones.
And the outbreak tallies are almost certainly an undercount, public health experts say.
US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before US President Donald Trump appointed him to oversee federal health agencies.
Kennedy and other federal leaders have argued that vaccination rates were waning for years before Trump took office a second time, that measles is not an “American phenomenon", and that the US government is handling measles better than other countries. In January, a US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) leader told reporters that the loss of the nation's elimination status would be the “cost of doing business” globally.
It's true that other countries are struggling with measles, and some also have lost their measles-elimination status. But public health experts and others say the outcome in the US wasn't inevitable.
“This humiliating determination is the tragic yet predictable result of an ongoing campaign by grifters, quacks and charlatans to put their own greed and self-worth ahead of the health and safety of children,” said Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.
The government has been taking some steps. In August and September, the CDC awarded $100 million to support state and local measles-response work. And Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz have made statements that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles from spreading.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” Schwartz said in a statement Tuesday. "We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities.”
But state and local health officials say the cost is far higher and that the moment demands a louder federal voice – and a bigger push for vaccinations – than Kennedy and Schwartz are providing.
“When the people at the front of the room are not speaking loudly and frequently in support of vaccination, the program starts to falter. And that’s what we’re seeing in the US,” said Noel Brewer, a University of North Carolina public health professor who chairs a committee that presented an analysis of US measles data to PAHO last week. “How many kids have to die before they start getting concerned?”
Some experts noted that neither Kennedy nor the CDC has scheduled a news conference to address their plans to fight measles. When the AP asked for Kennedy’s reaction to the US losing its measles-free status, an HHS spokesperson pointed to Schwartz’s statement. During the PAHO news conference, the health department did issue a news release promoting the latest episode of Kennedy’s online cooking show.

Russia’s Defence Ministry says preliminary findings on the crash point to equipment failure.
A military plane has crashed in western Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, according to a statement from the Russian Defence Ministry, cited by local media.
The Antonov An-12 transport aircraft went down in an unpopulated area near the city of Kemerovo, about 3,000km east of Moscow. The An-12 typically has a crew of six.
Air force experts were investigating the cause of the crash, but preliminary findings pointed to equipment failure.
“A commission from the Russian Aerospace Forces is working at the site to establish all the circumstances of the incident,” the ministry’s statement was quoted as saying by the RIA Novosti news agency.
Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had extinguished a fire. He said crews were helping to investigate the accident.
Seredyuk, in a video posted online showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when it crashed.
The Investigative Committee, Russia’s top criminal investigation agency, launched an inquiry into possible violations of flight safety rules, a standard practice following crashes.
The An-12 is a Soviet-built four-engine turboprop transport plane that has been in service since the late 1950s. More than 1,000 were built, and some still remain in operation in Russia and other nations.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that US authorities take "very seriously" any possible threat to Washington, following reports Iran was planning to target officials, possibly with a radioactive bomb.
Asked about the potential threat during a visit to the Philippines , Trump said: "If there is (such a threat), they will pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy."
CNN, citing seven anonymous US officials, reported that US intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb in Washington.
The report said the sources characterised Iran's plans as "an effort to give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack ".
A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive laced with chemical or radioactive materials.

texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y4:
Actress Gabrielle Creevy stars as Liz Rich, bringing "absolute authenticity to the role"
The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "frightening, inexplicable" things after moving to the countryside has been turned into a new TV drama.
The Witch Farm tells the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich who left London with their son Jonathan for a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start.
At first the isolation felt like freedom, but the family claimed things began to happen around the house leading them to feel increasingly scared.
Writer and creator, Danny Robins, met Liz who told him "her incredible story", becoming a four part series he beleives will "really surprise people".
Danny Robins hopes that new TV drama will raise the question, do ghosts exist?
Robins, who was also the executive producer of the project, explained how the idea for the four-part series came from a podcast he made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist , which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".
"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.
In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.
They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.
Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm .
"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.
After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.
The Witch Farm is based on the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich
Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.
"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."
He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.
Robins also hopes to raise the question – 'do ghosts exist?', sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.
"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.
The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy.
She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."
Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."
Creevy recently featured in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.
Robins said The Witch Farm is "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.
He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in it's creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."
The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday, 22 November.

Manuela Perteghella had criticised plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.
The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.
The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.
The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.
The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.
Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.
"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.
The planned move from Mason Croft has been paused while the university explores future options
The university said it would work with the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, institute staff, students, alumni and other partners over the coming months.
Tickell said the university's commitment to Shakespearean studies had "never been in doubt" but added that interest in studying in Stratford had remained low for several years.
He said related subjects had seen significant growth on the university's Birmingham campus, while the city's creative industries sector offered opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.
"Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students, and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England's greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Liberal Democrat MP Perteghella described the proposed move as "ill-thought" and "shocking".
She said she would raise the issue in Parliament and write to the university about her "deep disappointment" and concerns for the institute's future.
The University of Birmingham said it would spend the next six months exploring the centre's future
The MP backed a petition launched by the Stratford Herald calling on the university to keep the institute in Stratford-upon-Avon.
Actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman have also backed the campaign.
The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, was founded at Mason Croft in 1951 and has worked with academics, writers and performers including Dame Judi Dench.
